fixes.explanation: Celebrating sounds fun, but that's not the word. Jesus says, “…let us rest for a while.” The verse mentions no party at all. I think a quiet place with no crowd and no confetti sounds just right when people are coming and going and nobody has time to eat.

The text doesn't have them waiting. Many people saw the apostles leaving and recognized them, and they ran together on foot from all the towns. They arrived before Jesus and the apostles. A boat with a head start lost to people running, and I think that stings a little.

Going home is a fair guess. But Mark says many people saw them leaving and recognized them. They ran together on foot from all the towns and arrived before Jesus and the apostles. Those towns were where they ran from, friend, not where they went back to.

Mark says Jesus saw a large crowd and had compassion on them, because they were like sheep without a shepherd. Then He began to teach them many things. Notice the order: compassion first, then teaching. I think a shepherd leads, and Jesus starts leading with His words.

It's true, actually. The disciples do say it: “Dismiss the crowd so they can go to the surrounding countryside and villages and buy themselves something to eat.” They say it because it's a desolate place and the hour is already late. I think sending folks off to buy food sounds sensible, but Jesus has a different plan, friend.

Jesus tells them to go and see how many loaves they have. After checking, they say, “Five—and two fish.” Remember, they'd just asked whether to spend two hundred denarii to give all of them bread to eat. Next to that crowd, five loaves and two fish is far too little to go around.

Jesus directs them to have the people sit in groups on the green grass. They sat down in groups of hundreds and fifties. He gives that direction with only five loaves and two fish to work with. I think there's something calm about grass and orderly groups.

Lining up is a fair guess for a hungry crowd. But the text says Jesus directed them to have the people sit in groups on the green grass. They sat down in groups of hundreds and fifties. Nobody is told to line up.
You'd expect that from five loaves and two fish. But the text says they all ate and were satisfied. Hungry isn't the word Mark uses. All of them ate, friend, and all of them were satisfied.

That's a creative guess, but the text doesn't say it. It says they all ate and were satisfied. Satisfied means they had enough. I think a full stomach is hard to feel uneasy with, and I've tested that on cookie dough.

The disciples picked up twelve basketfuls of broken pieces of bread and fish. That came after everyone ate and was satisfied, and it all started with five loaves and two fish. Twelve baskets, friend. My leftovers after a long baking day fit in a single cookie tin.
